bib.title: Pre-train, Prompt, and Predict: A Systematic Survey of Prompting Methods in Natural Language Processing
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv v1, 28 Jul 2021; published ACM Computing Surveys 2023)

question: How can the prompt-based learning paradigm in NLP be formally described, organised along its design dimensions, and what are its applications and open challenges?
contributions: A unified mathematical notation (template, slots [X] and [Z], answer search, answer mapping) covering prompting work (Sec 2)
A typology along pre-trained model, prompt engineering, answer engineering, multi-prompt learning and training strategy (Fig 1)
Tables organising works on prompting (Tab 7-8), commonly used prompts (Tab 10), a timeline (Tab 12) and pre-trained LMs (Tab 13)
A meta-analysis of trends (Sec 11) and a list of challenges (Sec 10)
Companion website NLPedia-Pretrain with survey updates and paper list

results.claim: Largest pre-trained LMs listed in the appendix exceed 150B parameters (GPT-3, CPM-2, PanGu-alpha).
results.setup: Fig 7 sizes of 20 popular pre-trained LMs as of mid-2021
results.quote: GPT3, CPM2, and PanGu-α are the top three largest models with parameters greater than 150 billion.
results.note: Fig 7 values: GPT-3 175, CPM-2 198, PanGu-alpha 200 (billions), read from figure data in text

results.claim: Relation extraction has a much larger label space than binary sentiment, which makes answer engineering harder.
results.quote: (e.g. 80 in relation extraction v.s 2 in binary sentiment classiﬁcation)

results.claim: Adding a prompt is worth hundreds of labelled data points on average across classification tasks.
results.setup: classification tasks, Scao and Rush 2021 (not rerun here)
results.quote: adding prompts can achieve a similar accuracy improvement to the addition of 100s of data points on average across classiﬁcation tasks
results.where: Sec 9 data augmentation, p26; repeated Sec 10.6

results.claim: Choice of few-shot examples swings performance from near state-of-the-art to near random guess.
results.setup: Sec 6.2 sample selection; Lu et al. 2021
results.quote: ranging from near state-of-the-art accuracy on some tasks to near random guess (Lu et al., 2021)

results.claim: Prompt-based papers surged in 2021, attributed to GPT-3 (counts read from Fig 6a, not stated in text).
results.setup: Meta-analysis over the works in Tab 7-8 only (a hand-collected sample)
results.quote: We can see a huge surge in 2021, which is perhaps due to the prevalence of GPT-3

results.claim: Research shifted from discrete to continuous prompt search over time, with template search far more studied than answer search.
results.quote: there has been a shift from discrete search to continuous search for prompt engineering, as shown in Fig. 6-(d)

results.claim: Few-shot demonstrations can be biased by majority label, recency and common token (Zhao et al. 2021); calibrate with a context-free input such as N/A.
results.quote: three pitfalls (majority label bias, recency bias and common token bias)

results.claim: Prompts chosen with a larger validation set (tuned few-shot) transfer across similarly sized models, true few-shot-selected prompts do not, and transfer is poor across very different sizes.
results.quote: The transferability is poor when the model sizes are quite different in both scenarios.

limits: No experiments of its own: all findings are reported from cited work and are as of mid-2021 (pre-ChatGPT, no instruction tuning, RLHF, chain-of-thought, or tool use; GPT-3 is the largest model discussed, 175B)
Heavy focus on cloze prompts and masked LMs (BERT, RoBERTa, T5) and on classification and probing; task coverage reflects what was cheap to run
Authors concede few to no systematic comparisons across pre-trained LMs (Sec 10.5), tuning strategies (10.3), and little theory (10.6)
Meta-analysis counts only papers in Tab 7-8, a hand-selected sample
Internal inconsistency: Sec 8.5 says Jiang et al. 2020b found QA probabilities not very predictive of correctness, Sec 10.9 says the same work observed them well calibrated
Sec 7.1 notes that prompts built with annotated data are arguably not true zero-shot (Perez et al. 2021)
practices: Choose prompt shape by model: prefix prompts for left-to-right LMs and generation, cloze prompts for masked LMs, either for full-text-reconstruction models (Sec 4.1)
Select few-shot examples near the input in embedding space (Gao 2021; Liu 2021a KATE) rather than at random (Sec 6.2)
Order of demonstrations matters; score permutations, e.g. by entropy (Lu et al. 2021) (Sec 6.2)
Ensemble prompts by averaging probabilities, weighting by accuracy, or majority voting, to stabilise and reduce prompt-engineering cost (Sec 6.1)
Calibrate few-shot output with a context-free input to remove label, recency and token bias (Sec 10.9)
Allow several surface forms per label (answer paraphrasing, verbalizer sets) because surface forms compete for probability mass (Sec 5.2.2, 10.9)
Use prompt decomposition for token or span prediction (NER) and composition for span-relation tasks (Sec 10.4)

terms.definition: language models that model the probability of text directly; input x is modified by a template into a prompt x' with unfilled slots and the LM fills them to derive y
a textual string that has two slots: an input slot [X] for input x and an answer slot [Z] for an intermediate generated answer text z that will later be mapped into y
a prompt with a slot to fill in the middle of the text
a prompt where the input text comes entirely before z
Z is the set of permissible values for z; a mapping takes searched answer z to output y (several answers may map to one class)
a function from label y to a single answer token z
discrete: an actual text string; continuous: described directly in the embedding space of the LM, with its own tunable parameters
providing a few additional answered prompts that demonstrate how the LM should answer the actual prompt
the combination of tuning-free prompting and prompt augmentation
using multiple unanswered prompts for an input at inference time to make predictions

promptless fine-tuning; tuning-free prompting (LM frozen, no prompt params); fixed-LM prompt tuning (LM frozen, prompt params tuned); fixed-prompt LM tuning (LM tuned, prompt fixed); prompt+LM fine-tuning (both tuned)
zero training data for the task; very small number of training examples; reasonably large number of training examples
the process of creating a prompting function f_prompt(x) that results in the most effective performance on the downstream task
